questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests precise bit-twiddling without branches; validates wraparound understanding and constant-time composition.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation (circular shift)
- Modulo reduction via masking (k & 63)
- Safe right-shift with masking to avoid undefined behavior

## Code Example
```javascript
uint64_t rotateLeft64(uint64_t x, unsigned int k) {
  k &= 63;
  return (x << k) | (x >> ((64 - k) & 63));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you implement rotateRight64 using the same pattern?
- How would you vectorize this for an array of 64-bit words using SIMD intrinsics?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to reason about 128-bit bit patterns and leverage existing helper functions to implement non-trivial properties without using conditional branches.

## Key Concepts
- Bit reversal and palindrome detection in 128-bit space
- Constant-time, branchless implementation
- Integration with existing `reverse128` utility

## Code Example
```c
int isPalindrome128(uint64_t hi, uint64_t lo) {
  uint64_t rhi, rlo;
  reverse128(hi, lo, &rhi, &rlo);
  return (rhi == hi && rlo == lo);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend this approach to 256-bit values?
- What optimizations could be applied if the function were called frequently?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to apply simple bit-tricks succinctly and reason about edge cases without loops. It also shows understanding of bitwise adjacency relationships across 64 bits.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise AND and right shift
- Detecting pattern overlap without branching
- Constant-time evaluation on fixed width integers


## Why This Is Asked
Shows mastery of low-level bit tricks and edge-case handling in constrained environments.

## Key Concepts
- Next permutation with fixed popcount using bit hacks
- Branchless arithmetic for speed
- Fixed-width overflow behavior

## Code Example
```javascript
uint64_t nextHigherWithSamePopcount(uint64_t n) {
  uint64_t c = n & -n;
  uint64_t r = n + c;
  return (((n ^ r) >> 2) / c) | r;
}
```

## Why This Is Asked
This tests the ability to implement a branchless, 64-bit rotate using masking and shifts—a fundamental low-level technique in performance-critical code.

## Key Concepts
- 64-bit masking with &63 to constrain the rotation range
- Branchless rotation via (n >> r) | (n << (64 - r))
- Edge-case handling for k=0 without conditional branches

## Code Example
```javascript
function rotateRight64(n, k) {
  const r = k & 63;
  return (n >>> r) | (n << ((64 - r) & 63));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to arbitrary word sizes (e.g., 32-bit or 128-bit)?
- What are the trade-offs between rotate left and rotate right operations?
- How would this implementation behave on architectures with native rotate instructions?
